title: US Property and Casualty Insurers Post Their Best First-Quarter Underwriting Result in 25 Years, With an 89.5 Combined Ratio
summary: S&P Global Market Intelligence says the industry earned about $22.1 billion from underwriting in the first quarter of 2026, helped by a quiet catastrophe period, while competition in auto, falling commercial property rates and casualty claims inflation loom as headwinds.
description:
The US property and casualty insurance industry started 2026 with its best underwriting result for a first quarter in at least a quarter of a century, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. The analysis, based on company filings with the National Association of Insurance Commissioners as of May 19 and reported by Insurance Journal on May 22, shows an industry that was highly profitable in the first three months of the year, helped by a quiet period for catastrophes. It also shows where the pressure is building. The figures here are the industry aggregates from that report and are not forecasts.

The combined ratio is the key measure. It adds claims and expenses and divides by premiums, so a figure below 100 means an underwriting profit. The industry's combined ratio in the first quarter was 89.5 before policyholder dividends, the best first-quarter result in at least 25 years. Including policyholder dividends, which are payments made back to customers by some mutual insurers, it was 91.9, the best comparable result since 2006. The underwriting gain was about $22.1 billion, more than double the $10.2 billion of the first quarter of 2024 and above the inflation-adjusted $14.2 billion of the first quarter of 2006. S&P notes that the industry dividend ratio was nearly 2.4 points, the second highest in 25 years. State Farm's dividend of roughly $5 billion was recorded in the first quarter, while USAA's of roughly $4 billion was tied to 2025 results. For the full year 2025, the combined ratio was just under 93, the best in nearly two decades, with only 2006 at 92.4 better.

What drove the result? Mainly homeowners and private auto insurance. The homeowners multiperil loss ratio, meaning claims as a share of premiums, fell to 44.3 in the first quarter of 2026, from 102.3 in the first quarter of 2025, when the Los Angeles wildfires produced catastrophic losses. Other property lines, such as fire and the property part of commercial multiperil, also improved significantly. In private passenger auto, the largest personal line, the direct incurred loss ratio was 60.4. That was only 0.6 points lower than in the first quarter of 2025, but 15.4 points lower than in the first quarter of 2023, when the industry was struggling with rapid claims inflation. Seven of the biggest personal auto insurers, Progressive, Allstate, GEICO, State Farm, USAA, Farmers Group and Liberty Mutual, each posted an underwriting gain of more than $1 billion. State Farm's underwriting gain of nearly $2 billion contrasted with a loss of more than $5.0 billion in the first quarter of 2025, a swing of more than $7 billion.

The headline should not be read as a permanent change. A large part of the improvement compared with 2025 is the absence of a major catastrophe in the quarter. The wildfires that hit Los Angeles in early 2025 raised the base comparison, and a quieter period in 2026 lowered the loss ratio. Insurers' results swing with the weather, which is why a single strong quarter is a limited guide to the year.

S&P also flagged headwinds beneath the surface. Competition is mounting in private auto, which means insurers are fighting harder for customers, a development that tends to slow premium rises and can reduce margins. Commercial property rates are falling sharply, as capacity returns to the market. And casualty lines remain under pressure. The other liability loss ratio was 65.8, the highest first-quarter result in 24 years, and the direct incurred loss ratio for commercial auto liability was 71.1, up 3.2 points from the first quarter of 2025. These lines, which include general liability, umbrella and commercial auto, are exposed to what the industry calls social inflation, the rise in claims costs from larger jury awards, litigation funding and legal system practices. The reports reviewed here do not give a forecast for the full year.

How does this relate to more recent news? Travelers' third-quarter results, which we cover separately, show the same pattern in a later period: a strong underwriting margin with moderate catastrophe losses.  Taken together, the data show an industry that is currently profitable but whose margins depend on weather and on how casualty claims develop.

What does it mean for customers? Strong industry profits do not guarantee lower premiums, since prices reflect expected future costs, local conditions and each insurer's own results. They do suggest that insurers have room to compete, so shopping around may yield better offers in competitive lines such as private auto. In homeowners insurance, a quiet quarter does not remove the long-term pressure from severe weather and rebuilding costs. For businesses, falling commercial property rates may help renewals, while liability pricing could stay firm.

For investors and regulators, the main questions are how long the benign conditions last and whether competition erodes margins before casualty claims catch up. Rate adequacy, reserve strength and reinsurance costs will matter. This article reports on published industry statistics and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

The second-quarter figures, which S&P will publish in the late summer, will show whether the first quarter was an exception or the start of a longer run of strong results.
source_name: Insurance Journal (citing S&P Global Market Intelligence)
image_alt: US property casualty insurance industry underwriting profit combined ratio 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: S&P Global Market Intelligence reports a first-quarter 2026 combined ratio of 89.5 before policyholder dividends, the best first quarter in at least 25 years, and 91.9 including dividends, the best comparable result since 2006.

The underwriting gain was about $22.1 billion, driven mainly by homeowners multiperil and private auto; the homeowners loss ratio fell to 44.3 from 102.3 a year earlier, when Los Angeles wildfires struck.
Private passenger auto's direct incurred loss ratio was 60.4, down 0.6 points on a year earlier and 15.4 points below the first quarter of 2023.
Seven big personal auto insurers each earned underwriting gains above $1 billion, and State Farm's gain of nearly $2 billion compared with a loss of more than $5.0 billion a year earlier.

Headwinds include mounting competition in private auto, sharply falling commercial property rates and casualty pressure, with other liability's loss ratio at 65.8, the highest first-quarter result in 24 years.
why_it_matters: Insurer profits show whether prices are keeping ahead of claims. A record first quarter helps explain why some personal lines prices are flattening, but it also shows how much results depend on weather, and why casualty lines still face rising costs.

title: India's Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha Act: What the Law Changes for Insurers, Foreign Investors and Policyholders
summary: Parliament passed the Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill on December 16-17, 2025, raising the foreign investment limit in Indian insurers from 74% to 100% and giving IRDAI wider powers over intermediaries and boards.
description:
India has rewritten parts of its insurance law. The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill, 2025 was introduced and passed by the Lok Sabha on December 16, 2025, and passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2025, according to the tracker maintained by PRS Legislative Research, an independent organisation that summarises bills before Parliament. The law amends the Insurance Act of 1938, the Life Insurance Corporation Act of 1956 and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act of 1999. This article summarises the provisions listed by PRS. An earlier version of this article said the Act passed in January 2026 and described several measures, including details of the Bima Sugam marketplace, a risk-based capital timetable, an accounting standards deadline and a goods and services tax decision, that could not be verified against the sources reviewed, so they have been removed.

The most widely reported change is foreign ownership. The Bill raises the limit on foreign investment in Indian insurance companies from 74% to 100% of paid-up equity capital. That allows a foreign insurer to own an Indian subsidiary outright, where previously it needed an Indian partner or public shareholders for at least a quarter of the equity. The change matters for global insurers that want to expand in a market with a large population and relatively low insurance coverage.

A second change concerns reinsurance. The Bill reduces the net owned fund requirement for foreign reinsurers from ₹5,000 crore to ₹1,000 crore. Net owned funds consist of paid-up equity, free reserves, the balance in the share premium account and certain capital reserves, so the change lowers the capital a foreign reinsurer must hold in India to operate through a branch. The aim, as described in public discussion of the Bill, is to attract more reinsurance capacity to India, although PRS records the provision and not the motive.

The Bill also changes the rules for ownership transfers. The threshold above which a transfer of shares needs approval from the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) rises from 1% to 5% of the insurer's paid-up share capital. That reduces the number of routine transactions that need the regulator's clearance. For insurance co-operative societies, the Bill removes the ₹100 crore minimum paid-up share capital requirement for life, general and health insurance business.

On supervision, the Bill gives IRDAI more tools. It can approve schemes of arrangement between an insurer and a non-insurance company. It can supersede an insurer's board and appoint an Administrator where the insurer's business is prejudicial to the interests of policyholders. It can make regulations on the remuneration, commissions and disclosures of agents and intermediaries, and its powers of inspection and investigation extend to insurance intermediaries. The Bill adds managing general agents and insurance repositories to the existing list of intermediaries, which includes brokers, consultants and third-party administrators. In addition, the central government's power to modify or exempt insurers from the 1938 Act extends to International Financial Services Centres located in Special Economic Zones, and to the intermediaries operating there.

For policyholders, the Bill creates the Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund, which IRDAI administers to protect and educate policyholders. The fund is financed by government, institutional and other grants and donations, by penalties collected by IRDAI, and by other sums set out in regulations. The page does not specify how much will be in the fund or how it will be spent, which will depend on rules to be made.

What are the practical consequences? For foreign insurers, the change creates an option to build full-ownership businesses in India, though each decision will depend on rules, capital and returns, and it will take time to see whether any move. For domestic insurers and their partners, it could affect valuations and the terms of joint ventures, as foreign partners can in principle raise their stakes. For customers, any benefit depends on competition, product design and how well IRDAI uses its expanded powers; a rule change by itself does not lower premiums or speed up claims.

There are limits to what can be said from the sources. The PRS page does not give LIC-specific provisions, though the Bill amends the LIC Act, and it does not mention composite licences, which allow one company to sell life, health and general insurance. Readers interested in those topics should consult the text of the Act and IRDAI notifications, which will set the detail of implementation. Rules and regulations still need to be framed for many provisions, and the effect will depend on how quickly this happens.

The broader context is India's aim, expressed in the Act's title, of insurance for everyone. Low penetration, with many households underinsured against health and life risks, is the reason policymakers want more capital, more competition and stronger protections. Whether this law achieves that will be visible in the coming years in the number of new entrants, product prices, claims settlement records and complaint data published by the regulator.
image_alt: India IRDAI insurance regulatory reforms Bima Sugam digital marketplace 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: The Bill was introduced and passed by the Lok Sabha on December 16, 2025 and passed by the Rajya Sabha on December 17, 2025, according to PRS Legislative Research.
The foreign investment limit in Indian insurance companies rises from 74% to 100% of paid-up equity capital.
Net owned fund required of foreign reinsurers falls from ₹5,000 crore to ₹1,000 crore, and the IRDAI approval threshold for share transfers rises from 1% to 5%.

IRDAI gains power to supersede an insurer's board and appoint an Administrator where the business is prejudicial to policyholders, and to regulate commissions and disclosures of agents and intermediaries.
A Policyholders' Education and Protection Fund administered by IRDAI is created, funded by grants, donations and IRDAI penalty receipts.
why_it_matters: India is one of the world's fastest-growing insurance markets with low penetration. Allowing full foreign ownership and giving the regulator stronger powers affects who can invest, how insurers are supervised, and how customers are protected.

title: UAE Insurers Wrote Dh74.8 Billion of Premiums in 2025, With Health Cover Growing 16% After Mandatory Insurance Reached All Emirates
summary: Central Bank of the UAE data reported by Khaleej Times shows gross written premiums of Dh74.8 billion in 2025, up 14.9%, with health premiums of about Dh30 billion (up 16.3%), industry profit of Dh4 billion and a solvency ratio of 199%; mandatory basic health insurance for private-sector employees and domestic workers took effect across the emirates on January 1, 2025.
description:
The United Arab Emirates insurance industry grew strongly in 2025, and health cover was one of the main reasons. According to the Central Bank of the UAE's annual statistical report, reported by Khaleej Times on August 25, 2026, insurers wrote gross written premiums of Dh74.8 billion in 2025, an increase of 14.9% on the year before. Health insurance premiums were about Dh30 billion, up 16.3%. The year also saw the start of mandatory basic health insurance across all emirates for private-sector employees and domestic workers. This article draws on the Khaleej Times report of the central bank's data and on a Gulf News report from January 2025 about the nationwide scheme. We have not reviewed the central bank's report itself. Amounts are in UAE dirhams, which are pegged to the US dollar at about 3.67, so Dh74.8 billion is roughly $20.4 billion, our own conversion.

Start with the total. Of the Dh74.8 billion, property and liability premiums were Dh36.4 billion, up 14.1%, health Dh30 billion, up 16.3%, and life and fund accumulation Dh8.4 billion, up 12.1%. The article also gives line-by-line figures: motor and transportation of about Dh10.08 billion and fire of Dh6.89 billion. There is one inconsistency, which the article does not resolve. The business-line data gives health premiums of Dh36.42 billion, which differs from the Dh30 billion figure in the summary. The article says this version combines national and foreign insurers, but it does not explain the gap. Readers who need an exact health figure should consult the central bank's report. We use Dh30 billion as the headline number because it is the one stated alongside the growth rate.

What changed in health insurance? The Khaleej Times report says mandatory basic health insurance for private-sector employees and domestic workers took effect across the emirates on January 1, 2025. Gulf News, writing in January 2025, explained the background: Abu Dhabi and Dubai already required cover, and the scheme was being extended to Sharjah, Ajman, Fujairah, Ras Al Khaimah and Umm Al Quwain. Employers are required to provide the cover, and employees are expected to access group plans through them. An industry source named Vazayil, quoted by Gulf News, estimated that 30% to 40% of the market in the northern emirates already offered such cover, so the mandate added many new policyholders but did not start from zero. Gulf News did not give the price of the basic plan, who pays the premium or how the rule is enforced, so we do not state them. Some market reports say the cover is tied to visa issuance and set at a fixed basic package price, but we could not verify that from the sources reviewed.

The central bank data shows the effect in the policy counts and claims. Health policies rose 26.1%. Total policies across all lines were 17.3 million in 2025, up from 17.2 million, which is almost flat, so the 26.1% rise in health policies is not mirrored in the overall count; the article does not explain why. Claims paid across the industry were Dh46.2 billion, up 11%, and health claims rose 15.1%. The gross loss ratio, claims relative to premiums, improved to 65.1% from 68.9%, and the health loss ratio eased to 75.3% from 77.4%. A lower loss ratio means insurers kept more of each dirham of premium, which suggests that premium growth outpaced claims growth, though a loss ratio is only one part of profitability.

Profitability and strength improved. Industry profit was Dh4 billion, up from Dh2.6 billion in 2024, and the report attributes this mainly to higher net investment income. Invested assets were Dh96.4 billion, up 13.5%, or 58.4% of total assets. The solvency capital requirement ratio, a measure of how much capital insurers hold relative to what regulators require, was 199%, up from 196%. A ratio above 100% means the industry has more capital than the minimum. The market had 58 insurers in 2025: 22 national traditional insurers, 10 national takaful (Islamic) insurers and 26 foreign branches. Licensed insurance-related professions numbered 515, up from 495.

How does this compare with market-research estimates? Some research firms publish forecasts for the UAE health insurance market. One, Mordor Intelligence, puts it at $10.11 billion in 2026 and $15.04 billion by 2031, a compound growth rate of 8.26%. Those figures come from a commercial analyst, are forecasts and use their own definitions, so they cannot be compared directly with the central bank's reported premiums. We mention them as an indication of the expected direction only, and we could not verify the analyst's other claims, including market shares by emirate or distribution channel.

What does it mean for employers and residents? Employers in all emirates must now provide basic cover for eligible staff, which raises costs, particularly for firms in the northern emirates that had not offered it. Gulf News noted that employers may face rising costs from inflation and an ageing workforce, and that cost control and oversight are needed for the system to remain sustainable. For residents, the main benefit is wider access to a basic level of cover. For insurers, the combination of higher volumes, lower loss ratios and strong investment income made 2025 a good year, but the health loss ratio of 75.3% shows that health remains the most claims-intensive of the lines mentioned. Readers should check the central bank's website for the full report. This article is a news summary and not insurance advice.
source_name: Khaleej Times (Central Bank of the UAE annual statistical report) and Gulf News
image_alt: UAE Dubai health medical insurance market mandatory coverage growth 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Gross written premiums in the UAE reached Dh74.8 billion in 2025, up 14.9%: property and liability Dh36.4 billion (up 14.1%), health Dh30 billion (up 16.3%), life and fund accumulation Dh8.4 billion (up 12.1%).

Mandatory basic health insurance for private-sector employees and domestic workers took effect across the emirates on January 1, 2025; Abu Dhabi and Dubai already had schemes, and Gulf News listed Sharjah, Ajman, Fujairah, Ras Al Khaimah and Umm Al Quwain as the additions.
Health policies rose 26.1%, health claims rose 15.1% and the health loss ratio eased to 75.3% from 77.4%.
Industry profit rose to Dh4 billion from Dh2.6 billion, mainly because of higher net investment income; the solvency capital ratio was 199%, up from 196%.
The report's business-line table gives health premiums of Dh36.42 billion, which conflicts with the Dh30 billion headline and is not reconciled in the article.
why_it_matters: Health insurance is now one of the biggest premium lines in the UAE and the one most shaped by regulation. The data shows how much cover has expanded under the nationwide mandate, and how claims and loss ratios are responding as more people are insured.

title: Deloitte's 2026 Insurance M&A Outlook: A Selective, Disciplined Market With Private Capital in Specialty and Steady Life Dealmaking
summary: Deloitte expects 2026 insurance M&A to be disciplined and selective rather than a broad rebound, with eight themes including private capital in specialty lines, broker tuck-ins, AI-focused tech deals and cross-border inflows.
description:
Insurance dealmaking is returning, but with discipline, according to Deloitte's 2026 insurance M&A outlook. The consultancy says mergers and acquisitions in the sector showed renewed momentum in 2025, with more deal discussions and clearer market conditions, though few large headline deals closed. For 2026, Deloitte expects a selective market and not a broad rebound. This article summarises Deloitte's outlook. An earlier version of this article, built on secondary commentary, also said that M&A was being shaped by the rise of captives and alternative risk transfer, and that broker consolidation was under pressure. The Deloitte page we reviewed does not mention captives, so that point has been removed. The Deloitte page contains no deal counts, valuations or percentages, and this article therefore gives none.

What is behind the more cautious approach? Deloitte says insurers enter 2026 with stronger balance sheets and better visibility into their capital. Deals are aimed at profitable growth: scaling up, filling capability gaps and sharpening strategic focus. Insurers also use portfolio repositioning and divestitures to improve capital efficiency, meaning they sell or reinsure businesses that tie up capital without earning enough. Deal structures are becoming more flexible, and Deloitte notes that preparation may matter as much as appetite. The overall picture it paints is of a market gradually reopening, driven more by choice than urgency.

What are the eight expectations? First, selective M&A, with targeted, asset-light deals and divestitures. Second, private capital in specialty lines: specialty property and casualty, excess and surplus (E&S) lines, and managing general agents (MGAs) keep attracting private capital, with more scrutiny of underwriting quality. An MGA is a firm that underwrites insurance on behalf of insurers under delegated authority. Third, brokerage, where deals focus on integrating operations and adding small tuck-ins that deepen industry, regional or benefits expertise; cybersecurity and vendor oversight increasingly shape due diligence. Fourth, AI in technology deals: buyers target AI and analytics that improve underwriting, pricing and claims, rather than broad digital overhauls.

Fifth, life and annuities. Activity stays steady but quiet, centred on block deals, reinsurance and distribution, often with asset managers or private capital. A block deal transfers a group of existing policies to another insurer or reinsurer. Sixth, cross-border inflows: Japanese insurers and Middle Eastern capital keep flowing into the US market, and deals must fit US regulatory norms. Seventh, group insurance, where consolidation is episodic and scale matters for pricing, distribution and technology, so smaller players may consolidate or partner. Eighth, alternative capital: sidecars and structured partnerships add capacity and manage volatility, with more attention to capital clarity and risk transfer. A sidecar is a vehicle that lets investors take a share of an insurer's or reinsurer's risks and returns.

How does this fit with other developments? The cross-border theme matches a Fitch commentary covered on this site, which says Japanese insurers' major deals total about ¥4.5 trillion, 86% of it in the US, and that Korean insurers are also buying abroad. The specialty theme fits with WTW's survey, also covered here, that shows specialty rates falling back to 2020 levels as capacity increases. If prices keep softening, buyers of specialty businesses may become more cautious about valuations, though Deloitte's outlook does not make that prediction.

What does it mean for policyholders and businesses? Mergers can bring benefits, such as better technology and more capacity, but they can also reduce competition and cause changes in service, products or personnel. Customers of an acquired insurer typically continue under their existing contracts; changes are normally communicated by the insurer. Businesses that buy through brokers may see their broker acquired by a larger firm. They can ask about changes to service, fees and the insurers the broker uses.

What should readers watch? The key signals will be whether large strategic deals resume, how private capital responds to softer pricing in specialty lines, and whether regulators scrutinise cross-border or life-sector deals more closely. Deloitte frames its view as an outlook, not a forecast of particular transactions. Its comment that preparation may matter as much as appetite suggests that firms with clear priorities and integration plans will be better positioned.

What would change the picture? Deloitte's framing suggests several swing factors: a sharp catastrophe year that tests balance sheets, a move in interest rates that changes valuations of life books, regulatory objections to cross-border or private-capital deals, or a rush of capital into specialty lines that pushes prices below sustainable levels. The outlook does not assign probabilities to any of them. It also does not address the possibility of a downturn in insurer share prices, which could make acquisitions more or less attractive depending on valuations.

How should smaller companies read it? Deloitte notes that in group insurance, scale matters for pricing, distribution and technology, so smaller players may consolidate or partner. The same logic may apply to small brokers and MGAs, which face rising costs for cybersecurity and technology. Owners considering a sale or partnership would be wise to prepare their data, controls and governance in advance, since, as the outlook says, preparation may matter as much as appetite.

This article summarises a consulting outlook and is not investment advice. Deloitte is an adviser to many participants in these deals, and its view should be read with that in mind.
image_alt: Global insurance mergers acquisitions M&A strategic deals 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Deloitte says insurance M&A had renewed momentum in 2025 with more deal discussions and clearer conditions, though few large headline deals closed; it expects a disciplined, selective 2026 rather than a broad rebound.
Insurers enter 2026 with stronger balance sheets and better visibility into capital, and deals aim at profitable growth, capability gaps and strategic focus.
Private capital keeps flowing into specialty P&C, E&S and managing general agents, with more scrutiny of underwriting quality.
Brokerage deals focus on integration and small tuck-ins; buyers of technology target AI and analytics for underwriting, pricing and claims.
Cross-border inflows continue from Japanese insurers and Middle Eastern capital; life and annuity activity stays steady but quiet, centred on block deals and reinsurance.
why_it_matters: Mergers and acquisitions reshape who insures, advises and holds policyholder money. A disciplined market means fewer mega-deals, but steady restructuring that can affect competition, prices and the companies customers deal with.

title: Allianz Board Changes for 2027: Tomas Kunzmann to Oversee Asia Pacific, CFO Mandate Extended to 2031 as Klaus-Peter Röhler Retires
summary: Allianz announced on March 12, 2026 that Tomas Kunzmann joins its Board of Management from January 1, 2027, Klaus-Peter Röhler retires at the end of 2026, and CFO Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre's mandate is extended to 2031.
description:
Allianz has set out how its top team will look from 2027. The group announced on March 12, 2026, changes to its Board of Management that take effect on January 1, 2027, subject to regulatory approval where required. This article summarises Allianz's media release. An earlier version of this article, based on a secondary summary, said that Allianz was racing ahead of its three-year strategic roadmap and that Vienna Insurance Group had lifted profit above EUR 1 billion and proposed a 12% dividend increase. Neither statement appears in the Allianz release, so both have been removed.

Who is leaving? Klaus-Peter Röhler will retire from the Board on December 31, 2026, when his mandate expires and he reaches the age limit. He has served Allianz for 30 years. Michael Diekmann, Chairman of the Supervisory Board, thanked him for those 30 years of service. Oliver Bäte, the Group's chief executive, described him as an exceptional leader and a highly esteemed colleague. The release does not state which responsibilities he held, and this article does not guess.

Who is joining? Tomas Kunzmann, who has been chief executive of Allianz Partners, the group's assistance and travel insurance business, since July 1, 2022, joins the Board and takes responsibility for Asia Pacific, including India. He remains Allianz Partners chief executive until December 31, 2026, and a successor will be announced later. Kunzmann is 44. He joined Allianz in 2009, became a board member of Allianz Partners for Mobility and Assistance in 2020, and studied business administration at Friedrich Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg, according to the release. Bäte praised his growth and technology work at Allianz Partners.

How are responsibilities moving? Renate Wagner takes responsibility for Germany, Switzerland and Central Europe. She keeps her responsibility for People & Culture and for Mergers & Acquisitions, and she hands Asia Pacific to Kunzmann. Sirma Boshnakova becomes the reporting line for the Global Property & Casualty Retail unit. She already oversees Insurance Western & Southern Europe, Allianz Direct and Allianz Partners, which means her portfolio widens in retail P&C. The release does not give details of what the combination of these responsibilities means in practice, such as changes to teams or reporting lines below the Board.

What about the finance chief? Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre's mandate as chief financial officer is extended for five years, to December 31, 2031. For investors, this signals continuity in the role that oversees capital, reporting and financial targets. The release does not comment on strategy beyond the appointments.

Why is Asia Pacific important? The assignment of Asia Pacific, including India, to a member of the Board shows the region matters to the group. Elsewhere on this site, changes to insurance regulation in India are covered, including IRDAI's proposed amendments on registration and share transfers. The Allianz release does not discuss India strategy, so this article does not draw conclusions about it. The appointment of a manager from Allianz Partners, which operates globally in travel and assistance, may bring experience in international operations, but that is an observation about his background and not a statement by the company.

What is the wider context? European insurers have had strong results in recent years, and leadership succession is an important part of keeping that going. Planned retirements and multi-year mandate extensions are standard governance tools that give boards time to arrange succession and signal stability to shareholders and regulators. The release states that the changes are subject to regulatory approval where required, which is common for board appointments at large financial groups.

What should readers watch? The main open point is who will succeed Kunzmann at Allianz Partners, which the company says will be announced later. The group's results and updates to its targets will show whether the new structure changes priorities. The release does not give financial information.

What does this mean for customers? Board changes of this kind rarely affect policyholders directly. Contracts and claims continue as before. They may affect the strategic direction of the group over time, particularly in markets where the group is expanding.

How are board changes decided? Under German corporate law, the Supervisory Board appoints the members of the Board of Management, and the chairman of the Supervisory Board, here Michael Diekmann, usually announces such decisions. Appointments of insurance group directors are also subject to the regulator's fit-and-proper review, which explains the phrase about regulatory approval in the release. Announcing the changes nine months before they take effect gives time for the handover, in particular at Allianz Partners, where a successor still needs to be named.

Why do succession plans matter? For a group of Allianz's size, leadership continuity affects investor confidence and the execution of long-term strategy. The planned retirement of a board member who has served 30 years is a predictable event that boards prepare for, and the release presents it as an orderly one.

This article summarises a company announcement and is not investment advice.
source_name: Allianz SE media release (March 12, 2026) and Beinsure
image_alt: Allianz European insurance group board leadership changes corporate 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Effective January 1, 2027 (subject to regulatory approval where required), Tomas Kunzmann, CEO of Allianz Partners since July 2022, joins the Board of Management and takes responsibility for Asia Pacific, including India.
Klaus-Peter Röhler retires from the Board on December 31, 2026 after 30 years at Allianz, when his mandate expires and he reaches the age limit.
Renate Wagner takes responsibility for Germany, Switzerland and Central Europe, keeping People & Culture and Mergers & Acquisitions, and hands Asia Pacific to Kunzmann.
Sirma Boshnakova becomes the reporting line for the Global Property & Casualty Retail unit, in addition to Western & Southern Europe, Allianz Direct and Allianz Partners.
CFO Claire-Marie Coste-Lepoutre's mandate is extended by five years to December 31, 2031; Kunzmann remains Allianz Partners CEO until the end of 2026 and a successor will be announced later.
why_it_matters: Allianz is Europe's largest insurer, so changes at the top show how it plans to run its businesses in Asia and Europe. Continuity in the finance role and a planned succession suggest an orderly transition.

title: French Health Insurtech Alan Raises €100 Million (About $116 Million) at a €5 Billion Valuation, With €785 Million in Annual Recurring Revenue
summary: TechCrunch reported on March 11, 2026 that Alan raised €100 million led by Index Ventures at a €5 billion (about $5.83 billion) valuation, with 2025 ARR of €785 million up 53% and operational profitability in France.
description:
Alan, the French digital health insurer, has raised fresh funding at a valuation of €5 billion. TechCrunch reported on March 11, 2026, that the company raised €100 million, or about $116 million, in a round led by its existing investor Index Ventures. The valuation of €5 billion is about $5.83 billion, up from $4.5 billion in 2024. This article summarises TechCrunch's report. An earlier version of this article dated the raise to June and described it as a sign that the venture market was cautious. The report we reviewed dates it to March 2026 and does not discuss the venture market, so both points have been corrected. The figures for revenue and losses are reported by TechCrunch from the company, and we have not seen audited accounts.

Who invested? New investors are Greenoaks, Kaaf and SH. The round also included business angels, including Shopify founder Tobi Lütke and the 2018 FIFA World Cup winner Antoine Griezmann. Belfius, a strategic partner that led the previous Series F, also took part. Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve, the chief executive and co-founder, said the company can invest ambitiously, particularly in technology and AI. The article also names international expansion and product improvements as priorities.

How big is the business? Alan was founded in 2016 and has a team of 740 people. It serves 1 million employees, freelancers and retirees. Annual recurring revenue, or ARR, which is a measure of the yearly value of recurring subscriptions or premiums, reached €785 million, about $915 million, in 2025. That is up 53% from the end of 2024. The company aims for $1.16 billion in ARR in 2026, prioritising growth over profitability. It also won a contract to provide health insurance to up to 135,000 civil servants and their relatives.

Is Alan profitable? The company says it has reached operational profitability in France, its home and largest market, without disclosing exact figures. It says it is approaching operating break-even overall. Net losses were $61 million in 2023 and $56 million in 2024, and Alan says it has halved its losses as a percentage of revenue over the past 12 months. Because Alan has not disclosed net profit for 2025 in the report, we cannot say whether the company made a profit last year. Operating break-even and net profit are different measures, and readers should not treat them as the same.

Where does it operate? Alan operates in France, Belgium, Spain and Canada. In Canada, it is licensed in all provinces and has begun commercial operations. In Spain, its clients include HP and Volkswagen. TechCrunch notes that Alan was the first new independent insurance company licensed in France since the 1980s. That is a notable regulatory achievement, as insurance licensing is demanding and capital requirements are high. The chief executive is also a co-founding adviser and board member at the French AI company Mistral AI, according to the report.

What does it mean for the insurtech sector? Alan's results contrast with many insurtechs that have struggled to combine growth and profitability. A valuation of €5 billion for a business with €785 million ARR implies a multiple of about 6.4 times ARR, a figure we calculated from the reported numbers and not one that the company or its investors have stated. Such multiples depend heavily on growth expectations, and they can change quickly if growth slows.

What are the risks? Health insurance is regulated and heavily dependent on claims experience. Because its customers include corporate clients and a public-sector contract, it depends on those buyers continuing to purchase from it, and on regulators in each country. Expanding into new markets is costly and may reduce margins in the short term. Using AI in member service and claims raises questions about accuracy and privacy, particularly as the German court ruling on Google's AI Overviews, covered on this site, shows legal uncertainty over AI-generated statements. The TechCrunch report does not discuss these risks directly.

What should customers know? Employees covered through Alan can check their plan's benefits and the claims process with their employer. Alan's growth does not change the terms of any specific contract.

How does Alan's model work? According to the report, Alan's customers include employees, freelancers and retirees, and corporate clients such as HP and Volkswagen in Spain. It is part of a wider shift from traditional insurers and brokers to digital-first health insurers. The company's licence in France matters, because it means Alan carries insurance risk on its own balance sheet instead of acting only as an intermediary, though the report does not describe its reinsurance arrangements.

What else did the report say? Alan won a contract to provide health insurance to up to 135,000 civil servants and their relatives, which is a significant public-sector customer. It also said that growth in 2026 remains the priority over profitability, which means investors should expect continued spending on expansion.

This article summarises press reporting of a private company's funding round. It is not investment advice.
